claim: The peptidoglycan cell wall is an essential structural and morphological feature of most bacterial cells.
source: Although the peptidoglycan cell wall is an essential structural and morphological feature of most bacterial cells, the extracytoplasmic enzymes involved in its synthesis are frequently dispensable under standard culture conditions.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about bacterial cell walls.

claim: Extracytoplasmic enzymes involved in peptidoglycan synthesis are frequently dispensable under standard culture conditions.
source: Although the peptidoglycan cell wall is an essential structural and morphological feature of most bacterial cells, the extracytoplasmic enzymes involved in its synthesis are frequently dispensable under standard culture conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge in the field.

claim: A subset of 'redundant' enzymes in Escherichia coli are required for maximal fitness across pH environments.
source: By modulating a single growth parameter—extracellular pH—we discovered a subset of these so-called 'redundant' enzymes in Escherichia coli are required for maximal fitness across pH environments.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PBP1a and PBP1b are class A penicillin binding proteins that are pH specialists.
source: Among these pH specialists are the class A penicillin binding proteins PBP1a and PBP1b; defects in these enzymes attenuate growth in alkaline and acidic conditions, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing differential growth defects across pH conditions.

claim: Defects in PBP1a attenuate growth in alkaline conditions.
source: Among these pH specialists are the class A penicillin binding proteins PBP1a and PBP1b; defects in these enzymes attenuate growth in alkaline and acidic conditions, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by growth rate measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Defects in PBP1b attenuate growth in acidic conditions.
source: Among these pH specialists are the class A penicillin binding proteins PBP1a and PBP1b; defects in these enzymes attenuate growth in alkaline and acidic conditions, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by growth rate measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Synthase activity is required for cell wall integrity across a wide pH range.
source: Genetic, biochemical, and cytological studies demonstrate that synthase activity is required for cell wall integrity across a wide pH range and influences pH-dependent changes in resistance to cell wall active antibiotics.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches including genetic, biochemical, and cytological studies.

claim: Synthase activity influences pH-dependent changes in resistance to cell wall active antibiotics.
source: Genetic, biochemical, and cytological studies demonstrate that synthase activity is required for cell wall integrity across a wide pH range and influences pH-dependent changes in resistance to cell wall active antibiotics.
evidence: This is supported by antibiotic susceptibility testing data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Previously thought to be redundant enzymes are instead specialized for distinct environmental niches.
source: Altogether, our findings reveal previously thought to be redundant enzymes are instead specialized for distinct environmental niches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing pH-dependent specialization.

claim: Enzyme specialization may ensure robust growth and cell wall integrity in a wide range of conditions.
source: This specialization may ensure robust growth and cell wall integrity in a wide range of conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Escherichia coli occupies and grows in diverse environmental niches, including the gastrointestinal tract, bladder, freshwater, and soil.
source: A commensal, pathogen, and environmental contaminant, Escherichia coli occupies and grows in diverse environmental niches, including the gastrointestinal tract, bladder, freshwater, and soil.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli ecology.

claim: E. coli exhibits robust proliferation across a wide range of temperature, salt, osmotic, pH, oxygenation, and nutrient conditions in the laboratory.
source: In the laboratory, the bacterium's flexibility in growth requirements is reflected in robust proliferation across a wide range of temperature, salt, osmotic, pH, oxygenation, and nutrient conditions (Ingraham and Marr, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The periplasmic space of Gram-negative bacteria is sensitive to chemical and physical perturbations, including changes in salt, ionic strength, osmolality, and pH.
source: Due to the discrepancy in permeability between the plasma and outer membrane (Rosenbusch, 1990), the periplasmic space of Gram-negative bacteria is sensitive to chemical and physical perturbations, including changes in salt, ionic strength, osmolality, and pH.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Upon mild environmental acidification, the periplasm assumes the pH of the extracellular media.
source: Notably, upon mild environmental acidification, the periplasm assumes the pH of the extracellular media (Slonczewski et al., 1981; Wilks and Slonczewski, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mechanisms that contribute to cytoplasmic pH homeostasis have been described in detail.
source: Although mechanisms that contribute to cytoplasmic pH homeostasis have been described in detail (Castanie-Cornet et al., 1999; Castanié-Cornet et al., 2010), comparatively little is known about the quality control mechanisms that preserve proper folding, stability, and activity of key proteins in the periplasm.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Comparatively little is known about the quality control mechanisms that preserve proper folding, stability, and activity of key proteins in the periplasm.
source: Although mechanisms that contribute to cytoplasmic pH homeostasis have been described in detail (Castanie-Cornet et al., 1999; Castanié-Cornet et al., 2010), comparatively little is known about the quality control mechanisms that preserve proper folding, stability, and activity of key proteins in the periplasm.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: PG is essential for viability among most bacteria.
source: Essential for viability among most bacteria, PG is composed of glycan strands of repeating N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid disaccharide units crosslinked at peptide stems (Vollmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: PG is composed of glycan strands of repeating N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid disaccharide units crosslinked at peptide stems.
source: Essential for viability among most bacteria, PG is composed of glycan strands of repeating N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid disaccharide units crosslinked at peptide stems (Vollmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PG structure supported by a citation.

claim: The cell wall provides a force necessary to resist turgor pressure.
source: Beyond providing a force necessary to resist turgor pressure, the cell wall maintains cell shape, and components of the cell envelope serve as a major interface for cell-cell and cell-host interactions (Typas et al., 2012; McDonald et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The cell wall maintains cell shape.
source: Beyond providing a force necessary to resist turgor pressure, the cell wall maintains cell shape, and components of the cell envelope serve as a major interface for cell-cell and cell-host interactions (Typas et al., 2012; McDonald et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Components of the cell envelope serve as a major interface for cell-cell and cell-host interactions.
source: Beyond providing a force necessary to resist turgor pressure, the cell wall maintains cell shape, and components of the cell envelope serve as a major interface for cell-cell and cell-host interactions (Typas et al., 2012; McDonald et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PG synthesis is the principle target of several classes of antibacterial agents, including β-lactam and glycopeptide antibiotics.
source: As an essential process, PG synthesis is also the principle target of several classes of antibacterial agents, including β-lactam (e.g. penicillin) and glycopeptide (e.g. vancomycin) antibiotics.
evidence: This is established knowledge about antibiotic mechanisms.

claim: PG precursors are assembled in the cytosol and translocated across the inner membrane into the periplasm.
source: PG precursors are assembled in the cytosol and translocated across the inner membrane into the periplasm, where cell wall synthases construct the PG network through a series of glycosyltransferase (glycan polymerizing) and transpeptidase (peptide crosslinking) reactions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PG biosynthesis.

claim: Cell wall synthases construct the PG network through glycosyltransferase and transpeptidase reactions.
source: PG precursors are assembled in the cytosol and translocated across the inner membrane into the periplasm, where cell wall synthases construct the PG network through a series of glycosyltransferase (glycan polymerizing) and transpeptidase (peptide crosslinking) reactions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PG biosynthesis.

claim: PG synthases include bifunctional class A penicillin binding proteins, monofunctional transpeptidases (class B PBPs), and monofunctional glycosyltransferases of the SEDS protein families.
source: PG synthases include bifunctional class A penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), as well as monofunctional transpeptidases (class B PBPs) and monofunctional glycosyltransferases of the shape, elongation, division, and sporulation (SEDS) protein families (Sauvage et al., 2008; Meeske et al., 2016; Cho et al., 2016; Taguchi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: LD-transpeptidases synthesize non-canonical LD-crosslinks between peptide stems.
source: LD-transpeptidases synthesize non-canonical LD-crosslinks between peptide stems.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LD-transpeptidase function.

claim: LD-transpeptidases are predominately active during PG remodeling during stationary phase growth in E. coli.
source: They are predominately active during PG remodeling during stationary phase growth in E. coli (Pisabarro et al., 1985; Magnet et al., 2007) and are required under severe envelope stress (Morè et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LD-transpeptidases are required under severe envelope stress.
source: They are predominately active during PG remodeling during stationary phase growth in E. coli (Pisabarro et al., 1985; Magnet et al., 2007) and are required under severe envelope stress (Morè et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Periplasmic cell wall hydrolases and autolysins are required to accommodate nascent strand insertion for expansion of the PG network, create substrate binding sites, and separate cells during the final stages of cytokinesis.
source: In addition to synthases, a series of periplasmic cell wall hydrolases and autolysins—including DD-carboxypeptidases, DD and LD-endopeptidases, lytic transglycosylases, and amidases—are required to accommodate nascent strand insertion for expansion of the PG network, create substrate binding sites, and separate cells during the final stages of cytokinesis (Typas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Cell wall hydrolases may play a role activating synthases to ensure cell wall integrity.
source: These enzymes may also play a role activating synthases to ensure cell wall integrity (Lai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation.

claim: The periplasmic steps of PG synthesis and remodeling exhibit high levels of enzymatic redundancy.
source: The periplasmic steps of PG synthesis and remodeling exhibit high levels of enzymatic redundancy, the function of which remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The cytoplasmic steps of PG precursor biogenesis in E. coli have nearly a 1:1 stochiometric ratio between reactions and enzymes (12 reactions: 14 enzymes).
source: While the cytoplasmic steps of PG precursor biogenesis in E. coli have nearly a 1:1 stochiometric ratio between reactions and enzymes (12 reactions: 14 enzymes), over 36 enzymes can carry out the nine reactions that take place in the periplasm (Pazos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Over 36 enzymes can carry out the nine reactions that take place in the periplasm.
source: While the cytoplasmic steps of PG precursor biogenesis in E. coli have nearly a 1:1 stochiometric ratio between reactions and enzymes (12 reactions: 14 enzymes), over 36 enzymes can carry out the nine reactions that take place in the periplasm (Pazos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The SEDS glycosyltransferase/bPBP pairs RodA/PBP2 and FtsW/PBP3 are required for lateral expansion of the cell wall and cell division, respectively.
source: Moreover, with the exception of the SEDS glycosyltransferase/bPBP pairs RodA/PBP2 and FtsW/PBP3 required for lateral expansion of the cell wall and cell division, respectively (Meeske et al., 2016; Cho et al., 2016), the remaining periplasmic cell wall enzymes appear to be nonessential.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The remaining periplasmic cell wall enzymes appear to be nonessential.
source: Moreover, with the exception of the SEDS glycosyltransferase/bPBP pairs RodA/PBP2 and FtsW/PBP3 required for lateral expansion of the cell wall and cell division, respectively (Meeske et al., 2016; Cho et al., 2016), the remaining periplasmic cell wall enzymes appear to be nonessential.
evidence: This is a statement about the current understanding in the field.

claim: Inactivation of an individual enzyme often fails to confer discernable growth or morphological phenotypes under standard culture conditions.
source: Inactivation of an individual enzyme—and in some cases, even multiple enzymes in the same class—often fails to confer discernable growth or morphological phenotypes under standard culture conditions (Singh et al., 2012; Nelson and Young, 2000; Heidrich et al., 2002; Suzuki et al., 1978; Heidrich et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Enzymes within a given class may be specialists for distinct environmental niches.
source: One model to account for the apparent redundancy of periplasmic cell wall proteins is that enzymes within a given class may be specialists for distinct environmental niches, thereby allowing bacteria to cope with the diverse chemical and physical properties that might affect protein stability and function in this compartment (Pazos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a model/hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: E. coli carboxypeptidase PBP6b plays a key role in maintenance of cell morphology during growth at pH 5.0.
source: Peters and colleagues demonstrated that E. coli carboxypeptidase PBP6b plays a key role in maintenance of cell morphology during growth at pH 5.0 (Peters et al., 2016b), while Castanheira et al. identified a PBP3 homolog in Salmonella Typhimurium that is preferentially involved in septation at low pH (Castanheira et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A PBP3 homolog in Salmonella Typhimurium is preferentially involved in septation at low pH.
source: Peters and colleagues demonstrated that E. coli carboxypeptidase PBP6b plays a key role in maintenance of cell morphology during growth at pH 5.0 (Peters et al., 2016b), while Castanheira et al. identified a PBP3 homolog in Salmonella Typhimurium that is preferentially involved in septation at low pH (Castanheira et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The lytic transglycosylase MltA exhibits maximal activity in acidic conditions in vitro.
source: Similarly, the lytic transglycosylase MltA exhibits maximal activity in acidic conditions in vitro (van Straaten et al., 2005), although whether this property is relevant in vivo remains unknown.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: 32 mutants across six classes of nonessential periplasmic cell wall enzymes were screened.
source: In screening 32 mutants across six classes of nonessential periplasmic cell wall enzymes, we determined that a subset of these enzymes is differentially required for fitness across pH environments.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: A subset of nonessential periplasmic cell wall enzymes is differentially required for fitness across pH environments.
source: In screening 32 mutants across six classes of nonessential periplasmic cell wall enzymes, we determined that a subset of these enzymes is differentially required for fitness across pH environments.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Disruptions in the activity of PBP1a and PBP1b conferred fitness defects in opposing pH ranges.
source: We find that disruptions in the activity of cell wall synthases PBP1a and PBP1b conferred fitness defects in opposing pH ranges that can be attributed in part to pH-dependent differences in enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing differential growth defects.

claim: The fitness defects of PBP1a and PBP1b can be attributed in part to pH-dependent differences in enzymatic activity.
source: We find that disruptions in the activity of cell wall synthases PBP1a and PBP1b conferred fitness defects in opposing pH ranges that can be attributed in part to pH-dependent differences in enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical activity assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: Synthase specialization has consequences for intrinsic resistance to β-lactam antibiotics in nonstandard growth conditions.
source: We further demonstrate that synthase specialization has consequences for intrinsic resistance to β-lactam antibiotics in nonstandard growth conditions.
evidence: This is supported by antibiotic susceptibility data in Figure 6.

claim: Strains were cultured to mid-exponential phase in buffered LB media (pH 6.9) then sub-cultured into fresh LB buffered to pH 4.8, 6.9, or 8.2 for growth rate analysis.
source: To determine the contribution of individual cell wall enzymes to pH-dependent growth, we cultured strains harboring deletions in genes encoding each of three class A PBPs, six LD-transpeptidases, five carboxypeptidases, four amidases, nine lytic glycosyltransferases, and six endopeptidases to mid-exponential phase (OD600 ~0.2–0.6) in buffered LB media (pH 6.9) then sub-cultured them into fresh LB buffered to pH 4.8, 6.9, or 8.2 for growth rate analysis.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: pH values 4.8, 6.9, and 8.2 were chosen as representative, physiologically relevant conditions E. coli cells encounter in the lower GI tract (pH 5–9) or urine (pH 4.5–8).
source: These pH values were chosen as representative, physiologically relevant conditions E. coli cells encounter in the lower GI tract (pH 5–9) or urine (pH 4.5–8) (Watson et al., 1972; Henderson and Palmer, 1912).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work describing physiological pH ranges.

claim: Preliminary hits were identified by a significant (>5%) decrease in early exponential phase mass doublings per hour in at least one pH condition compared to the parental strain.
source: Preliminary hits were identified by a significant (>5%) decrease in early exponential phase (OD6000.005–0.1) mass doublings per hour (DPH) in at least one pH condition compared to the parental strain.
evidence: This describes the criteria used for identifying pH-sensitive mutants.

claim: Five mutants met stringent criteria and displayed significant pH-dependent reductions in DPH.
source: Collectively, five mutants met these stringent criteria and displayed significant pH-dependent reductions in DPH.
evidence: This is a summary of the screening results.

claim: Loss of PBP1b (mrcB) abolished growth at pH 4.8.
source: Strikingly, loss of the bifunctional synthase PBP1b (mrcB) abolished growth at pH 4.8—over half a pH unit lower than the growth restrictive condition for the parental strain (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Growth of the ΔmrcB mutant was significantly attenuated (10–25% defect in DPH) at pH values between 5.1–5.9.
source: Growth of the ΔmrcB mutant was also significantly attenuated (10–25% defect in DPH) at pH values between 5.1–5.9 but was indistinguishable from the parental strain in neutral and alkaline pH (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: ΔmrcB mutant growth was indistinguishable from the parental strain in neutral and alkaline pH.
source: Growth of the ΔmrcB mutant was also significantly attenuated (10–25% defect in DPH) at pH values between 5.1–5.9 but was indistinguishable from the parental strain in neutral and alkaline pH (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: Pre-conditioning the ΔmrcB mutant in acidic media (pH 5.5) did not abrogate the growth rate defect.
source: Pre-conditioning the mutant in acidic media (pH 5.5) did not abrogate the growth rate defect (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), indicating that steady-state pH—rather than pH shock—underlies the defect in DPH.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Steady-state pH—rather than pH shock—underlies the defect in DPH for the ΔmrcB mutant.
source: Pre-conditioning the mutant in acidic media (pH 5.5) did not abrogate the growth rate defect (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), indicating that steady-state pH—rather than pH shock—underlies the defect in DPH.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pre-conditioning experiment.

claim: Mutants defective in MltA and MepS exhibited a specific defect in DPH in acidic media with growth attenuated by 5–15% at pH values at or below 6.2.
source: Mutants defective in production of lytic transglycosylase MltA and endopeptidase MepS (spr) also exhibited a specific, albeit less severe, defect in DPH in acidic media: their growth was attenuated by 5–15% compared to wild type cells at pH values at or below 6.2 (Figure 1B,C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: MltA was previously shown to have elevated enzymatic activity in acidic conditions in vitro.
source: Consistent with a role in acid tolerance, MltA was previously shown to have elevated enzymatic activity in acidic conditions in vitro (van Straaten et al., 2005), and cells defective for PBP1b or MepS production exhibit reduced colony growth on acidic agarose plates (Nichols et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cells defective for PBP1b or MepS production exhibit reduced colony growth on acidic agarose plates.
source: Consistent with a role in acid tolerance, MltA was previously shown to have elevated enzymatic activity in acidic conditions in vitro (van Straaten et al., 2005), and cells defective for PBP1b or MepS production exhibit reduced colony growth on acidic agarose plates (Nichols et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of PBP1a (mrcA) and MltG (yceG) impaired growth specifically in neutral and alkaline media.
source: We also identified two alkaline-sensitive mutants. Loss of the bifunctional synthase PBP1a (mrcA) and the lytic transglycosylase MltG (yceG) impaired, but did not abolish, growth specifically in neutral and alkaline media (Figure 1A,C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Loss of MltG was associated with a greater magnitude and range of growth impairment (pH 6.2–8.4) compared to ΔmrcA (pH 6.5–8.2).
source: Loss of MltG was associated with a greater magnitude and range of growth impairment (pH 6.2–8.4 compared to pH 6.5–8.2 for ΔmrcA).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data comparing the two mutants.

claim: Both ΔmrcA and ΔyceG mutants' growth was restored to wild-type levels in acidic media (pH <6.0) and at pH 9.0.
source: Both mutants' growth was restored to wild-type levels in acidic media (pH <6.0) and at pH 9.0 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Individual deletions in genes encoding six LD-transpeptidases, five carboxypeptidases, and four amidases failed to confer any pH-dependent defects in DPH.
source: Individual deletions in the genes encoding for the six LD-transpeptidases, five carboxypeptidases, and four amidases failed to confer any pH-dependent defects in DPH at any pH tested, consistent with either a limited role of these enzymes in exponential phase growth (Pisabarro et al., 1985; Magnet et al., 2007) or additional layers of redundancy (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: E. coli requires at least one class A PBP for viability during growth in standard culture conditions.
source: Indeed, E. coli requires at least one of these enzymes for viability during growth in standard culture conditions (Suzuki et al., 1978).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Cells defective in PBP1a (ΔmrcA) and PBP1b (ΔmrcB) displayed defects in DPH at discrete, non-overlapping pH ranges.
source: Consistent with this model, cells defective in PBP1a (ΔmrcA) and PBP1b (ΔmrcB) displayed defects in DPH at discrete, non-overlapping pH ranges (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: Loss of PBP1c (pbpC) did not result in a defect in DPH at any pH tested alone or in combination with cells defective for PBP1a or PBP1b.
source: Loss of PBP1c (pbpC), a third class A PBP with an unclear role in cell wall metabolism (Schiffer and Höltje, 1999), did not result in a defect in DPH at any pH tested alone or combination with cells defective for PBP1a or PBP1b (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating this enzyme does not play a role in pH-dependent growth under the conditions tested here.
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PBP1c does not play a role in pH-dependent growth under the conditions tested.
source: Loss of PBP1c (pbpC), a third class A PBP with an unclear role in cell wall metabolism (Schiffer and Höltje, 1999), did not result in a defect in DPH at any pH tested alone or combination with cells defective for PBP1a or PBP1b (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating this enzyme does not play a role in pH-dependent growth under the conditions tested here.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: LpoA and LpoB are outer membrane lipoprotein cofactors required for activity, but not expression or stability, of PBP1a and PBP1b, respectively.
source: To test this, we took advantage of two sets of mutants: 1) deletions in lpoA and lpoB—genes encoding outer membrane lipoprotein cofactors required for activity, but not expression or stability, of PBP1a and PBP1b, respectively (Typas et al., 2010; Paradis-Bleau et al., 2010; Egan et al., 2014; Lupoli et al., 2014), and 2) point mutations that inactivate PBP1b transpeptidase and/or glycosyltransferase activity but do not impact stability (Meisel et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Loss of LpoB mimicked the pH-dependent growth defects of loss of PBP1b.
source: Implicating PBP activity in growth across pH environments, loss of the cofactors LpoA and LpoB mimicked the pH-dependent growth defects of loss of the enzymes themselves. Analogous to cells defective for PBP1b, deletion of lpoB prevented growth at pH 4.8.
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deletion of lpoB prevented growth at pH 4.8.
source: Analogous to cells defective for PBP1b, deletion of lpoB prevented growth at pH 4.8.
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Loss of LpoA led to a significant defect in DPH between pH values 5.9–8.2.
source: Likewise, loss of PBP1a's cofactor LpoA led to a significant defect in DPH between pH values 5.9–8.2 (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of either Lpo protein did not perfectly recapitulate loss of its cognate class A PBP.
source: Interestingly, loss of either Lpo protein did not perfectly recapitulate loss of its cognate class A PBP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Figure 2A–C), suggesting the presence of additional relevant regulators in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing growth data of Lpo and PBP mutants.

claim: There may be additional relevant regulators of class A PBPs in vivo beyond LpoA and LpoB.
source: Interestingly, loss of either Lpo protein did not perfectly recapitulate loss of its cognate class A PBP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Figure 2A–C), suggesting the presence of additional relevant regulators in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that Lpo and PBP mutants have slightly different phenotypes.

claim: Production of wild-type PBP1b in trans restored growth of the ∆mrcB mutant at pH 4.8.
source: As expected, production of wild-type PBP1b in trans restored growth of the ∆mrcB mutant at pH 4.8; however, production of PBP1b variants rendering the transpeptidase (S510A, TP*), glycosyltransferase (E233Q, GT*), or both enzymatic activities inactive (TP*GT*) failed to complement growth (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by complementation data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Production of PBP1b variants with inactive transpeptidase, glycosyltransferase, or both activities failed to complement growth of the ∆mrcB mutant at pH 4.8.
source: As expected, production of wild-type PBP1b in trans restored growth of the ∆mrcB mutant at pH 4.8; however, production of PBP1b variants rendering the transpeptidase (S510A, TP*), glycosyltransferase (E233Q, GT*), or both enzymatic activities inactive (TP*GT*) failed to complement growth (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by complementation data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The E233Q mutation in the glycosyltransferase active site attenuates transpeptidase activity by 90%.
source: It should be noted that the mutation in the glycosyltransferase active site (E233Q) previously has been shown to attenuate transpeptidase activity by 90%, consistent with observations that PBP transpeptidase activity cannot be assayed in vitro in the absence of functional glycosyltransferase activity (Egan et al., 2014; Bertsche et al., 2005; Terrak et al., 1999; Born et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PBP transpeptidase activity cannot be assayed in vitro in the absence of functional glycosyltransferase activity.
source: It should be noted that the mutation in the glycosyltransferase active site (E233Q) previously has been shown to attenuate transpeptidase activity by 90%, consistent with observations that PBP transpeptidase activity cannot be assayed in vitro in the absence of functional glycosyltransferase activity (Egan et al., 2014; Bertsche et al., 2005; Terrak et al., 1999; Born et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Transpeptidase activity is critical for pH-dependent growth.
source: Thus, although our data demonstrate that transpeptidase activity is critical for pH-dependent growth, we cannot discern whether glycosyltransferase activity alone is required.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the complementation experiments.

claim: It cannot be discerned whether glycosyltransferase activity alone is required for pH-dependent growth.
source: Thus, although our data demonstrate that transpeptidase activity is critical for pH-dependent growth, we cannot discern whether glycosyltransferase activity alone is required.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the experimental design.

claim: Extensive PI incorporation was observed at one hour post-shift for PBP1b defective cells that underwent acid shock (pH 6.9 to pH 4.5).
source: Consistent with a lytic origin, extensive PI incorporation was observed at one hour post-shift for PBP1b and PBP1a defective cells that underwent acid (pH 6.9 to pH 4.5) or alkaline (pH 6.9 to pH 8.0) shock, respectively (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Extensive PI incorporation was observed at one hour post-shift for PBP1a defective cells that underwent alkaline shock (pH 6.9 to pH 8.0).
source: Consistent with a lytic origin, extensive PI incorporation was observed at one hour post-shift for PBP1b and PBP1a defective cells that underwent acid (pH 6.9 to pH 4.5) or alkaline (pH 6.9 to pH 8.0) shock, respectively (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: PI+ cells lacked cytoplasmic GFP signal, confirming bona fide lysis.
source: To confirm bona fide lysis, we transformed a plasmid expressing gfp in to the mutants and measured PI incorporation and loss of cytoplasmic GFP concurrently. Without exception, PI+ cells lacked cytoplasmic GFP signal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ∆mrcB cells began to incorporate PI by 30 min (~15% cells labeled) upon pH downshift, with ~95–100% of cells labeled by two hours post-shift.
source: Time lapse imaging of cells following pH shift shed light on lysis kinetics: upon pH downshift, ∆mrcB cells began to incorporate PI by 30 min (~15% cells labeled), with ~95–100% of cells labeled by two hours post-shift.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data.

claim: Negligible cell death was observed for the parental strain or for cells defective for PBP1a during equivalent acid shock.
source: Negligible cell death was observed for the parental strain or for cells defective for PBP1a during equivalent acid shock (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Up to 15% of ∆mrcA cells underwent lysis an hour following alkaline shift to pH 8.0.
source: Conversely, up to 15% of ∆mrcA cells underwent lysis an hour following alkaline shift to pH 8.0 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ∆mrcB and wild type cells exhibited minimal (<5%) or negligible cell death, respectively, in response to alkaline shift on agarose pads.
source: ∆mrcB and wild type cells exhibited minimal (<5%) or negligible cell death, respectively, in response to alkaline shift on agarose pads.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data.

claim: Prior to cell lysis, single cell growth rate of both mutants and the parental strain were similar at each pH condition.
source: Prior to cell lysis, single cell growth rate of both mutants and the parental strain were similar at each pH condition (Figure 3A,B), indicating lysis is the sole determinant of decreased DPH observed in bulk culture.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell growth rate data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Lysis is the sole determinant of decreased DPH observed in bulk culture for PBP1a and PBP1b mutants.
source: Prior to cell lysis, single cell growth rate of both mutants and the parental strain were similar at each pH condition (Figure 3A,B), indicating lysis is the sole determinant of decreased DPH observed in bulk culture.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the single-cell growth rate data.

claim: A high fraction of ∆mrcB cells lysed during division, often from a bulge emanating at the septum.
source: Time lapse imaging during acid shock revealed a high fraction of ∆mrcB cells lysed during division, often from a bulge emanating at the septum (Figure 4A, white arrows; Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Scanning electron microscopy confirmed the bulges were coincident with the septum in the ∆mrcB mutant.
source: Scanning electron microscopy confirmed the bulges were coincident with the septum in this mutant (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by SEM data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 55% of ∆mrcB mutants lysed at the septum following pH downshift.
source: Indeed, this analysis confirmed our observation: 55% of ∆mrcB mutants lysed at the septum following pH downshift with the remaining fraction associated with a non-septal bulge (17%) and no bulge (28%) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Lysis of ~60% of ∆mrcA cells during growth in alkaline pH was coincident with a non-septal bulge, typically emanating from the periphery.
source: In contrast, lysis of the ∆mrcA mutant during growth in alkaline pH was not associated with division, and instead, lysis of ~60% of the cells was coincident with a non-septal bulge, typically emanating from the periphery (Figure 4B,D; Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4B,D.

claim: Differences in lysis mechanism between PBP1a and PBP1b mutants may reflect distinct localization preferences of the enzymes or disparate weak regions in the PG across pH conditions.
source: These differences may reflect distinct localization preferences of the enzymes (Bertsche et al., 2006; Banzhaf et al., 2012) or disparate weak regions in the PG across pH conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Bulk protein levels of both class A PBPs were modestly reduced in acidic media.
source: Consistent with previous proteomic mass spectrometry data (Schmidt et al., 2016), bulk protein levels of both class A PBPs were modestly reduced in acidic media (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5C and citation to previous work.

claim: pH-dependent differences in production of class A PBPs did not suggest a correlation between either enzyme's levels and its contribution to fitness in a particular pH environment.
source: However, pH-dependent differences in production did not suggest a correlation between either class A PBP's levels and its contribution to fitness in a particular pH environment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the protein level data.

claim: GFP-PBP1a localized predominantly to the cell periphery at neutral pH.
source: Similar to previous reports (Bertsche et al., 2006; Paradis-Bleau et al., 2014), the fusion proteins exhibited discrete localization profiles at neutral pH: GFP-PBP1a localized predominantly to the cell periphery, while GFP-PBP1b was present at both the periphery and the septum.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data and citations to previous work.

claim: GFP-PBP1b was present at both the periphery and the septum at neutral pH.
source: Similar to previous reports (Bertsche et al., 2006; Paradis-Bleau et al., 2014), the fusion proteins exhibited discrete localization profiles at neutral pH: GFP-PBP1a localized predominantly to the cell periphery, while GFP-PBP1b was present at both the periphery and the septum.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data and citations to previous work.

claim: GFP-PBP1b localization did not noticeably differ across pH conditions.
source: Although GFP-PBP1b localization did not noticeably differ across pH conditions, GFP-PBP1a peripheral signal was reduced at pH 5.0, and the fusion adopted an irregular clustered distribution throughout the cell body (Figure 5A,B; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: GFP-PBP1a peripheral signal was reduced at pH 5.0, and the fusion adopted an irregular clustered distribution throughout the cell body.
source: Although GFP-PBP1b localization did not noticeably differ across pH conditions, GFP-PBP1a peripheral signal was reduced at pH 5.0, and the fusion adopted an irregular clustered distribution throughout the cell body (Figure 5A,B; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: At pH 4.8, PBP1a + LpoA exhibited little glycosyltransferase or transpeptidase domain activity.
source: Strikingly, at pH 4.8 PBP1a + LpoA exhibited little glycosyltransferase or transpeptidase domain activity; in this condition the majority of [14C]lipid II precursor was not polymerized (Figure 5D, peak 1).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: PBP1b + LpoB + FtsN maintained similar end-point activity across all tested pH conditions.
source: In contrast, PBP1b + LpoB + FtsN maintained similar end-point activity across all tested pH conditions (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: In the absence of their cognate activators, both PBP1a and PBP1b exhibited reduced rates of glycosyltransferase activity in acidic conditions.
source: Consistent with previous work on PBP1b (Egan et al., 2014), in the absence of their cognate activators, both PBP1a and PBP1b exhibited reduced rates of glycosyltransferase activity in acidic conditions.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and a citation.

claim: Co-incubation of PBP1b with LpoB and FtsN significantly increased its polymerization rate under all pH conditions.
source: However, co-incubation of PBP1b with LpoB and division protein FtsN significantly increased its polymerization rate under all pH conditions, while PBP1a exhibited poor activity even in the presence of LpoA (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: PBP1a exhibited poor glycosyltransferase activity even in the presence of LpoA.
source: However, co-incubation of PBP1b with LpoB and division protein FtsN significantly increased its polymerization rate under all pH conditions, while PBP1a exhibited poor activity even in the presence of LpoA (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: PBP1a-LpoA bound at KD value of 520 ± 49 nM at pH 6.9.
source: PBP1a-LpoA and PBP1b-LpoB bound at KD values of 520 ± 49 nM and 213 ± 22 nM at pH 6.9, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: PBP1b-LpoB bound at KD value of 213 ± 22 nM at pH 6.9.
source: PBP1a-LpoA and PBP1b-LpoB bound at KD values of 520 ± 49 nM and 213 ± 22 nM at pH 6.9, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Both PBP-Lpo KD values were ~2 fold higher at pH 8.2.
source: Both KD values were ~2 fold higher at pH 8.2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4), but affinity values could not be determined at pH 4.8 due to significant non-specific binding of both LpoA and LpoB to the chip.
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Affinity values for PBP-Lpo interactions could not be determined at pH 4.8 due to significant non-specific binding.
source: Both KD values were ~2 fold higher at pH 8.2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4), but affinity values could not be determined at pH 4.8 due to significant non-specific binding of both LpoA and LpoB to the chip.
evidence: This is a limitation of the SPR experiments.

claim: PBP1a activity is reduced in acidic conditions, rendering the cell reliant on PBP1b for cell wall integrity and viability.
source: Altogether, our data support a model in which PBP1a activity is reduced in acidic conditions, rendering the cell reliant on PBP1b for cell wall integrity and viability.
evidence: This is a model/conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: A 4 to 32-fold increase in MIC to a subset of β-lactams was observed at pH values < 6.0.
source: In support of our hypothesis, we observed a 4 to 32-fold increase in MIC to a subset of the tested β-lactams at pH values < 6.0 (Figure 6A; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cells displayed an increase in intrinsic resistance to compounds that specifically target PBP2 and PBP3 at low pH.
source: In particular, cells displayed an increase in intrinsic resistance to compounds that specifically target PBP2 and PBP3, class B PBPs that are essential for cell elongation and division, respectively (Kocaoglu and Carlson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data and a citation.

claim: Cells cultured in low pH media retained near-normal morphology in the presence of concentrations of cephalexin or mecillinam that led to filamentation or cell rounding at pH 7.0.
source: Consistent with acidic pH conferring a protective effect on the elongation and division machinery and previous reports (Goodell et al., 1976), cells cultured in low pH media retained near-normal morphology in the presence of concentrations of the compounds that led to either filamentation (cephalexin, CEX) or cell rounding (mecillinam, MEC) at pH 7.0 (Figure 6B,C; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B,C and a citation.

claim: Uropathogenic E. coli isolate UTI89 exhibited a comparable change in MIC to cephalexin and mecillinam at low pH during growth in both broth culture and in urine.
source: The pH-dependent change in intrinsic resistance was not limited to our laboratory strain: uropathogenic E. coli isolate UTI89 (Chen et al., 2006) exhibited a comparable change in MIC to both cephalexin (CEX) and mecillinam (MEC) at low pH during growth in both broth culture and in urine (Figure 6D; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 6D and a citation.

claim: Susceptibility to non-specific β-lactams, a class A PBP-targeting compound, or a protein synthesis inhibitor was not strongly pH-dependent.
source: In contrast, susceptibility to non-specific β-lactams (ampicillin, AMP; amoxicillin, AMX), a class A PBP-targeting compound (cefsulodin, CFS) (Kocaoglu and Carlson, 2015), or a protein synthesis inhibitor (chloramphenicol, CH) was not strongly pH-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Differences in drug susceptibility could not be attributed to pH-dependent changes in antibiotic stability, proton motive force, β-lactamase production, or outer membrane permeability.
source: To rule out alternative causes of antibiotic resistance, we confirmed that differences in drug susceptibility could not be attributed to pH-dependent changes in antibiotic stability, proton motive force, β-lactamase production, or outer membrane permeability (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 3.

claim: pH-mediated plasticity in the cell wall synthesis machinery influences intrinsic β-lactam sensitivity.
source: These findings suggest that pH-mediated plasticity in the cell wall synthesis machinery influences intrinsic β-lactam sensitivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antibiotic susceptibility data.

claim: Loss of PBP1b abolished resistance to cephalexin at pH 5.5.
source: Genetic analysis suggests that PBP1b activity is specifically required for pH-dependent resistance to β-lactam antibiotics. Strains defective for production of PBP1a, PBP1c, LdtD, LdtE, MepS, MltA, MltG, and PBP6b exhibited a similar increase in resistance to CEX at pH 5.5 as the parental strain (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A). In contrast, loss of PBP1b abolished resistance at pH 5.5 and in fact, slightly increased susceptibility to CEX (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Resistance to other PBP2 and PBP3 targeting compounds was eliminated or significantly reduced in cells defective for PBP1b.
source: This phenotype was not specific to CEX: resistance to other PBP2 and PBP3 targeting compounds was also eliminated or significantly reduced in cells defective for PBP1b (Figure 6—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4C.

claim: PBP1b enzymatic activity was required for resistance to cephalexin at low pH.
source: PBP1b enzymatic activity was required for resistance. Loss of the enzyme's cognate outer membrane lipoprotein LpoB or inactivation of its catalytic activity eliminated CEX resistance at low pH (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 3B; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data from LpoB and catalytic mutant experiments.

claim: Loss of LpoB or inactivation of PBP1b catalytic activity eliminated cephalexin resistance at low pH.
source: Loss of the enzyme's cognate outer membrane lipoprotein LpoB or inactivation of its catalytic activity eliminated CEX resistance at low pH (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 3B; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: A mutant with a comparable growth rate defect at pH 5.5 (ΔtolA) still displayed the same fold change in resistance to CEX at pH 5.5 as the parental strain.
source: Importantly, a mutant with a comparable growth rate defect at pH 5.5 (ΔmrcB 1.91 ± 0.02 DPH; ΔtolA 1.40 ± 0.04 DPH) still displayed the same fold change in resistance to CEX at pH 5.5 as the parental strain.
evidence: This is a control experiment to rule out that the resistance phenotype is simply due to slow growth.

claim: A mutant in PBP5 (ΔdacA) with increased sensitivity to CEX at neutral pH retained the resistance phenotype in acidic growth conditions.
source: Likewise, a mutant in PBP5 (ΔdacA) with increased sensitivity to CEX even at neutral pH, similar to ΔmrcB (Schmidt et al., 1981; García del Portillo and de Pedro, 1990), also retained the resistance phenotype in acidic growth conditions (Sarkar et al., 2010) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3D and citations.

claim: PBP1b plays a specific role in intrinsic β-lactam resistance in acidic media.
source: In sum, our findings point to a specific role for PBP1b in intrinsic β-lactam resistance in acidic media.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic and biochemical data.

claim: Failure to produce PBP1b in acidic media or PBP1a in more alkaline conditions reduced fitness and led to cell lysis.
source: Of the pH specialist enzymes identified, we focused on the bifunctional synthases PBP1a and PBP1b, which we find are required for cell wall integrity in distinct pH environments. Failure to produce PBP1b in acidic media (pH <5.9) or PBP1a in more alkaline conditions (pH 6.5–8.2) reduced fitness and led to cell lysis (Figure 2 and Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by growth and microscopy data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Lytic death is characteristic of class A PBP-deficient cells.
source: This lytic death is characteristic of class A PBP-deficient cells (Suzuki et al., 1978) and is consistent with their essential role in PG synthesis, perhaps by filling gaps in the PG foundation (Cho et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A recent study failed to observe major differences in global PG composition in E. coli cells grown in pH 7.5 and pH 5.0.
source: Importantly, a recent study failed to observe major differences in global PG composition in E. coli cells grown in pH 7.5 and pH 5.0 (Peters et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The differential requirement for the class A PBPs in growth across pH conditions is unlikely to be a consequence of altered cell wall structure or distinct enzymatic activity of the PBPs.
source: Hence, the differential requirement for the class A PBPs in growth across pH conditions is unlikely to be a consequence of altered cell wall structure or distinct enzymatic activity of the PBPs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited study showing no major PG composition changes.

claim: pH-dependent differences in class A PBP activity underlie their contribution to maximal fitness in distinct pH environments.
source: Instead, our data suggest that pH-dependent differences in class A PBP activity underlie their contribution to maximal fitness in distinct pH environments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biochemical activity data.

claim: The precise mechanism for reduced activity of PBP1a in acidic media remains unclear.
source: At present, the precise mechanism for reduced activity of PBP1a in acidic media remains unclear; possible causes include pH-dependent changes in structure, substrate binding, or catalysis, as well as reduced affinity to LpoA in acidic conditions.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current study.

claim: The depletion of PBP1a from the cell periphery in acidic media may reflect an inactive state of the protein in vivo.
source: Although further work is needed, the depletion of PBP1a from the cell periphery in acidic media may also reflect an inactive state of the protein in vivo (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the localization data.

claim: It remains unclear why PBP1a is required for maximal fitness in alkaline media.
source: Although this finding is consistent with our observation that PBP1b can partially compensate for loss of PBP1a in alkaline media (Figure 2), it remains unclear why PBP1a is required for maximal fitness in alkaline media.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of an unexplained observation.

claim: Additional factors in vivo, such as novel class A PBP regulators, may be responsible for the cell's preference for PBP1a in alkaline conditions.
source: Additional factors in vivo, such as novel class A PBP regulators, may be responsible for the cell's preference for PBP1a in alkaline conditions that are not recapitulated in our in vitro assays.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the unexplained observation.

claim: PBP1b exhibits reduced binding to radiolabeled penicillin in membrane extracts incubated in alkaline buffer relative to neutral or acidic conditions.
source: In support of this model, PBP1b exhibits reduced binding to radiolabeled penicillin in membrane extracts incubated in alkaline buffer relative to neutral or acidic conditions (Amaral et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Differences in the enzymes' localization and/or interaction partners may play a role in their pH specialization.
source: Alternatively, differences in the enzymes' localization and/or interaction partners may also play a role in their pH specialization.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation.

claim: PBP1a and PBP1b preferentially associate with specialized cell wall synthesis complexes essential for cell elongation and cell division, respectively.
source: For example, PBP1a and PBP1b preferentially associate with specialized cell wall synthesis complexes essential for cell elongation and cell division, respectively (Müller et al., 2007; Bertsche et al., 2006; Banzhaf et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Future work investigating the influence of pH on the essential components of the elongation and division machinery is necessary to determine whether the activity of these complexes affects the cell's class A PBP preference.
source: Our current study was limited to interrogating the pH specialization of nonessential cell wall enzymes. Future work investigating the influence of pH on the essential components of the elongation and division machinery is thus necessary to determine whether the activity of these complexes affects the cell's class A PBP preference.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: PBP1a and PBP1b share an essential role in growth and cell wall integrity under standard culture conditions.
source: Although PBP1a and PBP1b share an essential role in growth and cell wall integrity under standard culture conditions (i.e. nutrient rich, neutral pH growth medium) (Suzuki et al., 1978), there had been previous hints these enzymes were not interchangeable.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Each class A PBP possesses unique interaction partners and subcellular localization profiles.
source: As previously mentioned, each class A PBP possess unique interaction partners and subcellular localization profiles (Müller et al., 2007; Bertsche et al., 2006; Banzhaf et al., 2012; Gray et al., 2015; Leclercq et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutants defective for each class A PBP display differential susceptibility to antibiotic treatment, osmotic shifts, and mechanical stress.
source: Mutants defective for each enzyme also display differential susceptibility to antibiotic treatment (discussed below), osmotic shifts, and mechanical stress (Yousif et al., 1985; Paradis-Bleau et al., 2014; Auer et al., 2016) and have different roles in de novo regeneration of rod shape (Ranjit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Class A PBPs have different roles in de novo regeneration of rod shape.
source: Mutants defective for each enzyme also display differential susceptibility to antibiotic treatment (discussed below), osmotic shifts, and mechanical stress (Yousif et al., 1985; Paradis-Bleau et al., 2014; Auer et al., 2016) and have different roles in de novo regeneration of rod shape (Ranjit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Further study of 'redundant' cell wall autolysins under nonstandard culture conditions will continue to reveal unique roles for these enzymes in cell wall biogenesis.
source: We anticipate further study of these synthases—as with other 'redundant' cell wall autolysins—under nonstandard culture conditions will continue to reveal unique roles for these enzymes in cell wall biogenesis.
evidence: This is a prediction about future research.

claim: Environment-driven plasticity in E. coli PG synthesis may have consequences for intrinsic resistance to β-lactam antibiotics with a narrow target specificity.
source: Analogous to alternative PBP usage in methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (Berger-Bächi, 1999; Chan et al., 2016), our results suggest that environment-driven plasticity in E. coli PG synthesis may have consequences for intrinsic resistance to β-lactam antibiotics with a narrow target specificity (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antibiotic susceptibility data and supported by citations.

claim: Culturing E. coli in low pH media is sufficient to increase intrinsic resistance to PBP2 and PBP3-targeting β-lactams up to 32-fold.
source: Strikingly, we find that culturing E. coli in low pH media is sufficient increase intrinsic resistance to PBP2 and PBP3-targeting β-lactams up to 32-fold.
evidence: This is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 6.

claim: E. coli encounters a wide range of pH environments across host niches.
source: Considering E. coli encounters a wide range of pH environments across host niches (Watson et al., 1972; Bilobrov et al., 1990), our observation reinforces the importance of conducting antibiotic susceptibility testing under physiologically relevant conditions (Ersoy et al., 2017; Thulin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The observation reinforces the importance of conducting antibiotic susceptibility testing under physiologically relevant conditions.
source: Considering E. coli encounters a wide range of pH environments across host niches (Watson et al., 1972; Bilobrov et al., 1990), our observation reinforces the importance of conducting antibiotic susceptibility testing under physiologically relevant conditions (Ersoy et al., 2017; Thulin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an implication of the findings supported by citations.

claim: Low pH-dependent resistance specifically requires PBP1b activity.
source: Mechanistically, our data demonstrate low pH-dependent resistance specifically requires PBP1b activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic and biochemical data.

claim: Cells defective for PBP1b or LpoB are hypersensitive to a wide variety of β-lactams.
source: PBP1b has previously been implicated in intrinsic resistance to β-lactam antibiotics: cells defective for PBP1b or LpoB are hypersensitive to a wide variety of β-lactams (Nichols et al., 2011; Paradis-Bleau et al., 2014; García del Portillo and de Pedro, 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Elevated PBP1b activity protects cells from the lethality of the PBP2 specific antibiotic mecillinam.
source: Likewise, elevated PBP1b activity protects cells from the lethality of the PBP2 specific antibiotic mecillinam (Lai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The precise role for PBP1b in β-lactam protection remains unclear.
source: At present, the precise role for PBP1b in β-lactam protection remains unclear.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of current understanding.

claim: The role in β-lactam protection appears to be a function specifically endowed to PBP1b, as cells defective for PBP1a production do not display differential β-lactam susceptibility.
source: It appears to be a function specifically endowed to PBP1b, for cells defective for PBP1a production do not display differential β-lactam susceptibility (Nichols et al., 2011; García del Portillo and de Pedro, 1990), highlighting another possible source of specialization between the class A PBPs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PBP1b may play a role in preserving the normal functions of the elongation and division machinery in low pH environments.
source: Interestingly, we and others have observed cells cultured in acidic media exhibit near normal morphology in the presence of concentrations of PBP2 or PBP3 inhibitors that lead to cell rounding or filamentation at neutral pH (Figure 6B,C) (Goodell et al., 1976). We thus speculate that PBP1b may play a role in preserving the normal functions of the elongation and division machinery in low pH environments.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the morphology data.

claim: PBP1b may substitute for the essential function of PBP2 and PBP3 in elongation and division complexes.
source: PBP1b may substitute for the essential function of PBP2 and PBP3 in these complexes (Modell et al., 2014) or may indirectly support growth by serving a quality control function (Morè et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative model supported by citations.

claim: PBP1b may indirectly support growth by serving a quality control function.
source: PBP1b may substitute for the essential function of PBP2 and PBP3 in these complexes (Modell et al., 2014) or may indirectly support growth by serving a quality control function (Morè et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative model supported by a citation.

claim: Clarifying PBP1b's role in intrinsic resistance to β-lactams will shed light on the mechanics of cell wall biogenesis and inform the design and use of novel antibiotic therapies.
source: Clarifying PBP1b's role in intrinsic resistance to β-lactams will shed light on the mechanics of cell wall biogenesis and inform the design and use of novel antibiotic therapies.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of future research.

claim: Environmental specialization of cell wall enzymes is likely a key adaptation that allows E. coli to thrive across an unusually wide pH range (pH ~4–9).
source: Apart from influencing antibiotic resistance, environmental specialization of cell wall enzymes is likely a key adaptation that allows E. coli to thrive across an unusually wide pH range (pH ~4–9) and even tolerate extreme pH shocks, such as during transient exposure to gastric acid (pH ~2) (Jordan et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an inference about the broader significance of the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: E. coli can tolerate extreme pH shocks, such as during transient exposure to gastric acid (pH ~2).
source: Apart from influencing antibiotic resistance, environmental specialization of cell wall enzymes is likely a key adaptation that allows E. coli to thrive across an unusually wide pH range (pH ~4–9) and even tolerate extreme pH shocks, such as during transient exposure to gastric acid (pH ~2) (Jordan et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Plasticity in the cell wall synthesis machinery likely works in concert with the organism's ability to modify extracellular pH through the export of acidic and alkaline substrates.
source: Plasticity in the cell wall synthesis machinery likely works in concert with the organism's ability to modify extracellular pH through the export of acidic and alkaline substrates (Lu et al., 2013; Krulwich et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative model supported by citations.

claim: pH-specialist cell wall enzymes may function in part to maintain cell wall integrity until the extracellular media reaches a growth-permissive pH.
source: In this context, pH-specialist cell wall enzymes may function in part to maintain cell wall integrity until the extracellular media reaches a growth-permissive pH.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the role of pH-specialist enzymes.

claim: Strategies employed to expand growth across wide pH ranges are likely to vary among pH tolerant organisms, even between closely related species.
source: Among other pH tolerant organisms, strategies employed to expand growth across wide pH ranges are likely to vary, even between closely related species.
evidence: This is a general statement about bacterial diversity.

claim: S. enterica serovar Typhimurium encodes a PBP3 paralog, termed PBP3SAL, that is active during growth in acidic environments, including intracellularly in the phagolysosome.
source: S. enterica serovar Typhimurium encodes a PBP3 paralog, termed PBP3SAL, that is active during growth in acidic environments, including intracellularly in the phagolysosome (Castanheira et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PBP3SAL is restricted to Salmonella, Enterobacter, and Citrobacter spp.
source: As PBP3SAL is restricted to Salmonella, Enterobacter, and Citrobacter spp., alternative mechanisms to cope with changing pH environments must exist.
evidence: This is a statement about the phylogenetic distribution of PBP3SAL.

claim: Alternative mechanisms to cope with changing pH environments must exist beyond PBP3SAL.
source: As PBP3SAL is restricted to Salmonella, Enterobacter, and Citrobacter spp., alternative mechanisms to cope with changing pH environments must exist.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limited distribution of PBP3SAL.

claim: Class A PBPs are broadly conserved across bacteria.
source: Elucidating the requirements for pH-dependent growth in organisms outside the Enterobacteriaceae will shed light on whether class A PBPs, which are broadly conserved across bacteria (Typas et al., 2010), play a central role in the process.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Enzyme specialists may exist across environmental conditions beyond pH.
source: Apart from pH, we anticipate enzyme specialists exist across environmental conditions; redundancy in cell wall enzymes is present throughout bacterial species, even among those that only grow at a narrow pH range (Pazos et al., 2017).

claim: Ionic strength, osmolality, and temperature vary across the diverse habitats bacteria occupy and may have significant impacts on the chemical and physical properties of the periplasm.
source: Ionic strength, osmolality, and temperature also vary across the diverse habitats bacteria occupy. Like pH, these factors may have significant impacts on the chemical and physical properties of the periplasm and the extracytoplasmic space of Gram-positive bacteria.
evidence: This is a general statement about bacterial physiology.

claim: PBP2 from Caulobacter crescentus displays differential localization patterns as a function of extracellular osmolality.
source: In support of this idea, PBP2 from Caulobacter crescentus displays differential localization patterns as a function of extracellular osmolality (Hocking et al., 2012), and the lytic transglycosylase MltA from E. coli is ~10 times more active at 30°C than at 37°C in vitro (van Straaten et al., 2005; Lommatzsch et al., 1997).
